title: Wandering for Christ
hook: Irish monks set out in boats without oars, going where God led

segments.voice: Yesterday, thin places: spots where heaven and earth seem to stand close together. Your line was heaven is thin here. Did a place, or a moment, go thin for you? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

Three men wash up on the coast of Cornwall in a little boat made of hides. The boat has no oars. An old English record, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, tells it in a few plain lines. They had slipped away from Ireland because they wanted to be on pilgrimage for the love of God, and they did not care where. They took food for about a week. They let the sea carry them. Then they were brought before King Alfred, who must have had questions. Nobody had steered. That was the whole point. Irish Christians had a Latin word for setting out like this, and today it's ours: peregrinatio. Wandering for Christ.
screen: `FOR THE LOVE OF GOD, THEY CARED NOT WHERE.`

segments.voice: In everyday Latin, peregrinatio meant living abroad, being the foreigner in town. Irish Christians gave it a sharper edge: leaving home on purpose, as an offering to God. Not a trip with a ticket back. An exile you chose. Some looked back to Abraham. In Genesis, God says to him: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee." No map. No name for the place. Just a promise. The letter to the Hebrews looks back on him and says "he went out, not knowing whither he went." A few verses on, it calls the people of faith "strangers and pilgrims on the earth." Some Irish monks took that line at its word. Columba left Ireland and settled on Iona; his biographer Adomnán says he sailed away wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ. Others, the stories say, pushed out with no plan and let the wind and the current choose the shore. A boat without oars sounds reckless. To them it was trust you could see. They gave up control, and on open water of all places. Where they landed, the stories go on, they prayed, and some of them built a small community and stayed for the rest of their lives. Christians read this old practice in more than one way. Some hear it as a call that came to a few, and still comes, to leave everything. Some walk long pilgrim roads for a season. And some hear it as a picture of the inner life: holding plans loosely, and saying yes to the place where you've been set down.

Here's the practice: let the wind choose one thing. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Bring today's plan to mind, the whole tight route of it, hour by hour. Now look for one small gap you could leave open. A different street home. A bench you've never sat on. A door you always walk past. Don't pick the destination. Just decide to go. Notice what happens in you as you loosen your grip on the oars, even a little. If you pray, you can hold the open space before God, the way Abraham set out. The bell holds the time.
Peregrinatio. Latin for living abroad; for the Irish saints, leaving home for the love of God and going where they were led.
Your line: where the wind takes. Today, go somewhere unplanned: one turn, one street, one stop you didn't schedule. See what's there. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians today go on walking pilgrimages, including to old Celtic sites such as Iona; others take the Irish idea of peregrinatio inwardly, as a way of holding their plans loosely and trusting God to lead.

notes: Claims rule: the boat of hides, no oars, food for about a week (the Chronicle says provisions for seven nights), landing in Cornwall and being brought to King Alfred all come from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry (s.a. 891). Confirm the details; the year is deliberately not stated.
The index hook says 'Irish monks'; the Chronicle calls them three Scots (i.e. Irishmen) and does not say they were monks, so the script says 'three men' and 'Irish Christians'.
'In everyday Latin, peregrinatio meant living abroad' is a lexical gloss (Lewis and Short: a sojourning or traveling in foreign parts). Confirm; no etymology is given.
Adomnán, Vita Columbae, second preface: 'pro Christo perigrinari volens enavigavit'. Confirm the paraphrase and the trapdoor's 'Latin verb from the same family' (peregrinari).
'Others, the stories say, pushed out with no plan' is attributed to stories, not stated as history.
Genesis 12:1 is spoken to Abram (his name before Genesis 17); the script uses the familiar name Abraham.
Previous ten days (1142–1151) had no scripts on disk when this was written; angles were checked against the index lines (Ignatian days, caim, Carmina Gadelica blessings, thin places).

Editor pass: 'Their model was Abraham' softened to 'Some looked back to Abraham'; 'the one thing everyone wants on open water' (sweeping claim) cut; the landing-and-staying line attributed to the stories; 'small island' dropped since day 1151 just described Iona that way.
